devices.whySpecs: The X1-Carbon reads your sliced 3MF/G-code from the microSD card and writes timelapse frames and logs back to it during the print. The bottleneck here is not raw speed, but reliability and data integrity. A single corrupt block on a cheap or worn card can stall or abort a multi-hour, multi-color AMS print that has already burned through real filament. Bambu ships the printer with a card and recommends formatting as FAT32; a name-brand A1/A2 card from SanDisk or Samsung in the 32-64GB range is the reliable sweet spot. Capacity is almost irrelevant (print files are only a few MB to tens of MB), so pay for a trustworthy card, not a huge one.

faq.q: Why did my Bambu X1-Carbon fail mid-print or say it can't read the file?
faq.a: The most common culprit is a cheap, counterfeit, or worn-out microSD card. The X1C reads the print file and writes timelapse/log data to the card, so a flaky card causes 'failed to load file' errors and mid-print stalls. Reformat as FAT32 and switch to a genuine SanDisk or Samsung card before blaming the printer.

faq.q: What size microSD card does the X1-Carbon need?
faq.a: 32GB is plenty. Sliced print files are only a few megabytes to tens of megabytes each. A 64GB card gives headroom for timelapses. Bambu recommends FAT32 formatting, which is simplest on cards up to 32GB; larger cards work but should be reformatted to FAT32 rather than the default exFAT.

faq.q: Do I need a fast U3/V30 card for the X1-Carbon?
faq.a: No. The X1C doesn't stream video to the card, so a standard Class 10 / U1 card is sufficient. Prioritize a reputable brand and the A1/A2 app-performance rating for reliability over a high V-class number. Speed ratings matter for cameras; integrity matters for 3D printers.

devices.notes: microSD (FAT32). Frame around reliability/integrity, not speed — failure mode is a corrupt read aborting a long AMS print. Recommend genuine name-brand A1/A2 cards, 32-64GB. Warn explicitly against counterfeit/cheap cards as the #1 cause of failed prints.

devices.name: FiiO SnowSky Echo Mini
devices.whySpecs: As a dedicated Digital Audio Player (DAP), the Echo Mini relies on the microSD card for its primary library. While audio playback bitrate is low (requiring only Class 10), database indexing requires fast random read speeds. An A1-rated card ensures that the retro UI remains snappy and album art loads instantly when scrolling through large libraries of FLAC or DSD files.

faq.q: What is the max SD card size for the SnowSky Echo Mini?
faq.a: Officially 256GB. However, like most FiiO players, it is widely reported to support 512GB and 1TB cards if they are formatted to FAT32. Using cards larger than the official limit may result in longer boot times while the device scans for music.

faq.q: Does the Echo Mini come with internal music storage?
faq.a: It includes 8GB of internal memory, which is sufficient for the OS and a small 'favorites' playlist. For a full high-resolution library, a microSD card is required.

devices.notes: FiiO sub-brand focused on retro cassette aesthetics. Features dual CS43131 DACs. Supports DSD, WAV, FLAC, APE.

devices.name: Sony Walkman NW-A306
searchTerms: best sd card for sony walkman
devices.whySpecs: The NW-A306 runs Android with 32GB of internal storage. Music libraries go on the card, and Android scans it to build your library. An A1 or A2 card speeds up those scans and any streaming app that caches to the card.

faq.q: Why is my Sony Walkman NW-A306 slow?
faq.a: Often the card. Android's media scan and app caches do many small random reads. A card with an A1 or A2 rating, such as the SanDisk Extreme, speeds that up.

faq.q: What is the maximum microSD capacity for the Sony NW-A306?
faq.a: 2TB. Many owners use 1TB cards for large FLAC and hi-res libraries.

devices.notes: The current market standard for compact Android Hi-Res players. Card performance directly impacts UI fluidity.

devices.name: Sony Walkman NW-ZX707
devices.whySpecs: The NW-ZX707 is the high-end sibling to the A306, featuring a larger screen and better amplification. Like the A306, it runs Android and requires an A2-rated card for smooth operation. Users of this device typically have massive DSD/FLAC libraries, making 1TB cards a very common choice.

faq.q: Does the ZX707 have internal storage?

devices.notes: Premium Android DAP. Often purchased by users upgrading from the A306 who need more power for headphones.

devices.name: HiBy R3 II
devices.whySpecs: A direct competitor to the SnowSky Echo Mini. The HiBy R3 II runs a lightweight proprietary OS (HiByOS) and has no internal storage for music. A reliable microSD card is mandatory. It is known for fast card scanning, so standard Class 10 / U1 cards work well, though A1 cards are still preferred for album art loading.

faq.q: Does the HiBy R3 II function without an SD card?
faq.a: No, not for local playback. It has no internal storage for music files. Without a card, it can only act as a Bluetooth receiver or USB DAC.

devices.notes: Budget-friendly audiophile player. Often praised for its 'MSEB' sound tuning features.

devices.name: HiBy R4
devices.whySpecs: The HiBy R4 is a mid-range Android 12 DAP with a distinct 'Cyberpunk' industrial design. Because it runs open Android and supports streaming apps, it shares the same requirement as Sony Walkmans: an A2-rated card is highly recommended to keep the system snapping and responsive.

faq.q: Is the HiBy R4 better than the R3 II?
faq.a: They are different categories. The R4 runs Android, allowing you to install Spotify/Apple Music, but it is larger and heavier. The R3 II is a pure music player (no apps) that is much smaller. Both need SD cards.

devices.notes: Released in 2024. Very trendy 'Cyberpunk' aesthetic. High value-for-money Android DAP.

devices.name: Astell&Kern A&norma SR35
devices.whySpecs: The SR35 is the entry-level premium player from Astell&Kern. It features Quad DACs and a unique tilted screen. While it has 64GB internal storage, the high-res files (DSD/MQA) it is designed to play require massive storage. A reliable name-brand card is essential for the custom UI stability.

faq.q: Does the SR35 run Android?
faq.a: It runs a heavily modified, closed version of Android. You cannot install the Play Store, but it supports whitelisted streaming apps (Tidal, Spotify, etc.). An A1 or A2 card is recommended for best app performance.

devices.notes: Entry-level luxury DAP. Known for the 'tilted' screen design and exceptional Quad DAC audio quality.

devices.name: Zoom H1n-VP Handy Recorder
devices.whySpecs: Critical Warning: The Zoom H1n (and H1n-VP) is an older hardware architecture that does NOT support cards larger than 32GB. Users frequently buy 64GB or 128GB cards that fail to work. You must use a microSDHC card (32GB or smaller). Speed is not critical; compatibility is.

faq.q: Why does my Zoom H1n say 'Invalid Card' or 'No Card'?
faq.a: You are likely using a card that is too large. The Zoom H1n has a strict hardware limit of 32GB. It cannot read 64GB, 128GB, or larger cards (microSDXC). You must purchase a 32GB microSDHC card.

faq.q: How many hours of audio fits on a 32GB card?
faq.a: A 32GB card can hold over 15 hours of highest-quality WAV audio (24-bit/96kHz) or over 500 hours of MP3 audio. For a dedicated audio recorder, 32GB is a vast amount of space.

devices.notes: One of the most popular portable recorders in the world. The 32GB limit is the #1 source of user confusion and support searches.

devices.name: Zoom H6 Handy Recorder
devices.whySpecs: The Zoom H6 uses full-size SD cards. While it is a powerful recorder, it is known to be picky with cards larger than 128GB. Zoom officially recommends formatting cards inside the device to ensure stability. Class 10 is sufficient for 6-track recording.

faq.q: Does the Zoom H6 support 256GB cards?
faq.a: Not officially. Zoom lists 128GB as the maximum tested capacity. While some users report success with larger cards, stick to 128GB or smaller for professional reliability.

devices.notes: The industry standard for field recording and podcasting. Uses Full-Size SD cards (unlike the H1n which uses microSD).

devices.name: Tascam DR-05X
devices.whySpecs: Unlike the Zoom H1n, the Tascam DR-05X supports the newer microSDXC format, allowing for cards up to 128GB. Tascam recorders are notoriously picky about card formatting, so using a high-quality name-brand card and formatting it inside the recorder is essential to prevent 'Write Timeout' errors.

faq.q: Does the Tascam DR-05X support 256GB cards?
faq.a: No, the official maximum supported capacity is 128GB. While some users attempt to use larger cards, Tascam firmware is strict, and using unsupported capacities creates a high risk of file corruption during long recording sessions.

devices.notes: Popular stereo handheld recorder. Supports larger cards than the Zoom H1n, but caps at 128GB.

devices.name: Zoom H4essential
devices.whySpecs: The H4essential records multitrack 32-bit float WAV, which produces large files. Zoom supports microSDHC from 4GB to 32GB and microSDXC up to 1TB. A U3/V30 card handles the sustained write.

faq.q: What is the maximum SD card size for the Zoom H4essential?
faq.a: 1TB, using a microSDXC card. The official manual specifies microSDHC support from 4GB to 32GB and microSDXC support up to 1TB, and that 1TB ceiling is the number to plan around for long 32-bit float multitrack sessions.

faq.q: Do I need a fast card for 32-bit float recording on the H4essential?
faq.a: Yes, use a U3/V30-rated card. Recording up to 6 simultaneous tracks in 32-bit float WAV produces a high sustained data rate. A V30 card keeps pace without dropped frames or write errors during long sessions.

devices.notes: Newer flagship handheld Zoom recorder. 32-bit float multitrack recording with a stated 1TB microSDXC ceiling — the specific data point this audience searches for.

devices.name: Tascam Portacapture X6
devices.whySpecs: The Portacapture X6 is a 6-track stereo recorder capable of up to 96kHz/32-bit floating point recording, and Tascam officially supports microSDXC cards up to 512GB. Multitrack 32-bit float projects at high sample rates fill cards quickly, so the practical buying advice is to size up (256GB-512GB) rather than buy the smallest card that fits a single session. A V30-rated card comfortably handles the sustained 6-track write load.

faq.q: What is the maximum SD card size for the Tascam Portacapture X6?
faq.a: 512GB, using a microSDXC card. That's the official ceiling, so there's no need to shop for 1TB cards for this device, but a 256GB-512GB card is worth the upgrade over a smaller one given how fast 6-track 32-bit float projects fill storage.

faq.q: How is the Portacapture X6 different from the Tascam DR-05X?
faq.a: The X6 is a 6-track multitrack recorder; the DR-05X is stereo-only. The X6 targets musicians and field recordists building multitrack projects at up to 96kHz/32-bit float, which needs far more storage headroom than the DR-05X's simple stereo WAV files.

devices.notes: 6-track multitrack recorder, distinct from the simpler stereo-only DR-05X already on the site. 512GB official capacity ceiling is the key search data point.

devices.name: Canon EOS R5

The SD UHS-II slot needs a V90 card for standard 8K, while V60 is enough for 4K. High bitrate video demands fast, dual card slots for safety.

faq.q: Do I need two cards for the Canon R5?
faq.a: No, but it's safer. The R5 has a CFexpress Type B slot and an SD UHS-II slot. Recording to both gives you a backup, but only the CFexpress card handles 8K RAW.

faq.q: Can I shoot 4K on the R5 with V30 cards?
faq.a: For standard 4K IPB, yes. 8K on SD needs V90, and 8K RAW needs CFexpress Type B.

faq.q: What's the difference between CFexpress and SD in the R5?
faq.a: Speed. CFexpress Type B writes over 1,000 MB/s and handles 8K RAW. A V60 or V90 SD UHS-II card costs less and covers 4K.

devices.notes: Canon EOS R5 is professional 8K camera. Dual V60 cards strongly recommended.
devices.metaDescription: The Canon EOS R5 records 8K RAW only to CFexpress Type B. On SD UHS-II, V90 covers 8K IPB and V60 covers most 4K. Best cards for each slot.

faq.q: Does the Sony A6700 have two card slots?

devices.name: Sony A7 IV

sdCard.type: CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II

devices.whySpecs: The A7 IV records high-bitrate 4K video. Slot 1 accepts ultra-fast CFexpress Type A cards or SD cards, while Slot 2 is SD-only. A V60 SD card is needed for most 4K modes, while V90 is required for the highest quality S&Q (Slow & Quick) recording to prevent buffer issues.

faq.q: Do I need a CFexpress Type A card for the Sony A7 IV?
faq.a: No, it's not required for most shooting. A V60 or V90 SD UHS-II card is sufficient for almost all video modes. CFexpress Type A is only necessary for clearing the buffer faster during intense burst photography or for the absolute highest video bitrates.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two card slots?
faq.a: Slot 1 is a combo slot that fits either one CFexpress Type A card or one SD card (UHS-I/II). Slot 2 only fits one SD card (UHS-I/II). You can use both for simultaneous backup or relay recording.

devices.notes: Extremely popular camera. Note: Your sdcards.json has limited V60+ SD card options, so only compliant cards are recommended.

devices.name: Canon EOS R6 Mark II
searchTerms: eos r6 mark ii memory card
devices.whySpecs: The R6 Mark II features two SD UHS-II card slots. For video recording at up to 42.5 MB/s bitrate, a V60 card is sufficient. However, for high-speed burst shooting at 40fps with RAW, V90 cards are recommended to clear the buffer quickly and prevent missed shots.

faq.q: Do I need two cards for the R6 Mark II?
faq.a: It is highly recommended for professional work. Using both slots allows for instant backup, overflow (relay) recording, or separating file types (e.g., RAW to Slot 1, JPEG to Slot 2). For casual use, one card is sufficient.

faq.q: Is V60 enough, or do I need V90?
faq.a: For video: V60 is sufficient. For burst shooting: V90 is recommended. If you shoot both, V90 provides the best performance across all modes. V60 cards offer better value if you primarily shoot video or landscapes.

devices.notes: Supports both UHS-I and UHS-II cards, but UHS-II is strongly recommended for optimal performance.

devices.name: Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera 4K

faq.q: Which card type should I use for the BMPCC 4K?
faq.a: It depends on your codec. For the highest quality Blackmagic RAW settings (e.g., 3:1), you will need a CFast 2.0 card. For more compressed RAW formats and most ProRes options, a fast V90 SD card will suffice and is more cost-effective.

devices.notes: A staple for indie filmmakers with very specific card requirements. Both CFast 2.0 and V90 SD card options are now recommended for maximum flexibility.

devices.name: Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera 6K Pro
devices.whySpecs: The BMPCC 6K Pro records professional 6K RAW and ProRes at extremely high bitrates. CFast 2.0 is required for the highest quality 6K RAW formats, while SD UHS-II V90 cards can handle high-quality ProRes and some compressed RAW codecs.

faq.q: Do I need CFast for the BMPCC 6K Pro?
faq.a: For full 6K RAW recording, yes. CFast 2.0 is essential for the highest bitrate 6K RAW codecs. However, for recording in DCI 4K or many ProRes formats, a fast SD UHS-II V90 card will work and is more affordable.

devices.notes: Professional-grade 6K cinema camera. Both CFast 2.0 and V90 SD card options are now recommended for maximum flexibility.

faq.q: Which card slot should I use on the Nikon Z8?
faq.a: Use the CFexpress slot for maximum performance, especially for 8K video or long bursts of high-resolution photos. Use the SD slot for backup, overflow, or for less demanding 4K video work.

devices.notes: Often called the 'baby Z9', it packs flagship performance into a smaller body, with demanding media requirements to match.

faq.q: Is V90 required for the Panasonic S1H?
faq.a: For 6K and All-Intra modes, yes. V60 cards handle lower-bitrate modes, but the camera blocks the high-bitrate ones without V90.

devices.notes: A professional 6K hybrid camera. Now that Sony TOUGH G V90 has been added to your sdcards.json, it is the recommended card.

devices.name: Fujifilm X100VI

faq.q: Can I use my old X100V cards in the X100VI?
faq.a: Yes, if they are V30. Both cameras have UHS-I slots, and V30 covers the X100VI's 200 Mbps top bitrate.

faq.q: Do I need a V60 or V90 card for the X100VI?
faq.a: No. The top bitrate is 200 Mbps (25 MB/s), which V30 covers, and the UHS-I slot can't use UHS-II speed.

devices.notes: The most hyped camera of 2024. Known for its retro design and exceptional image quality. Extremely high search volume for accessories due to its popularity and limited availability.

devices.whySpecs: An advanced APS-C mirrorless camera designed for sports and wildlife photography, featuring 15fps burst shooting and 4K 60fps video. A V60 speed class card is highly recommended for reliable 4K 60fps recording and sustained high-speed burst shooting to prevent buffer overflow.

faq.q: Do I need V60 or is V30 enough for the R7?
faq.a: V60 is strongly recommended for the EOS R7. While V30 cards may work for some 4K modes, the R7's advanced capabilities, such as 4K 60fps and 15fps RAW burst shooting, generate a significant amount of data that requires the sustained write speeds of V60 cards to ensure smooth performance and prevent dropped frames.

faq.q: Should I use both SD card slots?

devices.notes: Canon's flagship APS-C mirrorless camera. Very popular with wildlife and sports photographers seeking high performance without the full-frame cost. Features dual SD UHS-II slots.

faq.q: R10 vs R50 - do I need faster cards?

faq.q: Is the R8 Canon's cheapest full-frame camera?

faq.q: Can I use V30 cards in the R8 to save money?

devices.notes: Canon's budget-friendly full-frame option. Popular with hybrid shooters who need both strong photo and video capabilities in a compact form factor. Features a single SD UHS-II card slot.

devices.notes: Canon's best-selling beginner DSLR. Extremely high search volume due to its popularity with photography students and first-time camera buyers. A very cost-effective option for learning the fundamentals of photography.

searchTerms: canon g7x mark ii sd card
devices.whySpecs: The previous generation of Canon's popular vlogging compact, capable of 1080p 60fps video. Class 10 (U1) cards are perfectly sufficient for all its recording modes, as it does not shoot 4K. This model remains popular on the used market as a budget-friendly option for aspiring vloggers and casual photographers.

faq.q: Should I upgrade from the Mark II to the Mark III?
faq.a: Only if you specifically need 4K video recording or live streaming capabilities. The G7 X Mark II is still an excellent camera for 1080p vlogging and photography, often available at a significantly lower price on the used market. You can save money on both the camera body and SD cards, as V30 cards are not required.

faq.q: Do I need V30 cards for the Mark II?
faq.a: No, Class 10 (U1) cards are perfectly sufficient for the G7 X Mark II. As this camera's maximum video resolution is 1080p, it does not require the higher sustained write speeds offered by V30 cards. You can save money by using standard, reliable Class 10 cards.

devices.notes: Still very popular on the used market. High search volume from budget-conscious vloggers and photographers seeking an affordable alternative to the newer Mark III model.

devices.name: Fujifilm X-T5

sdCard.minSpeed: V60 (V90 recommended for high bitrate video)

devices.whySpecs: Fujifilm's flagship APS-C camera, featuring a 40MP sensor and capable of 6.2K 30fps video recording. A V60 card handles most photography and 4K video shooting, but a V90 card is recommended for the highest bitrate 6.2K recording and sustained 15fps RAW bursts. Its dual SD slots enable professional workflow options like backup recording and overflow.

faq.q: Do I need V90 cards for the X-T5, or is V60 enough?
faq.a: V60 cards are sufficient for most users and all typical photography needs on the X-T5. V90 cards only provide a tangible benefit if you are consistently shooting 6.2K video at the highest bitrate settings or require extended RAW burst shooting with minimal buffer limitations. For general photo and 4K video work, V60 cards offer excellent performance.

faq.q: Should I use both SD card slots?
faq.a: Yes, for professional work or any important photography/videography sessions, it is highly recommended to utilize both dual UHS-II card slots. You can configure them for instant backup (simultaneous writing to both cards), overflow (recording continues to the second card when the first fills), or to separate file types (e.g., RAW files to one card, JPEGs to the other), which significantly enhances reliability and streamlines post-production workflow.

devices.notes: Fujifilm's current APS-C flagship camera. Extremely popular with enthusiast photographers and professionals due to its image quality and classic controls. Features dual SD UHS-II slots for robust media management.

devices.name: Fujifilm X-M5
devices.whySpecs: A compact, vlogging-focused APS-C camera capable of 6.2K video recording. Despite its entry-level positioning, the high-resolution video output necessitates V30 cards for reliable recording without dropped frames. The use of a UHS-I slot helps keep the camera's size and cost down while still supporting advanced video features.

faq.q: Is the Fujifilm X-M5 Fujifilm's cheapest X-mount camera?
faq.a: Yes, the X-M5 is positioned as Fujifilm's most affordable interchangeable lens camera. It is specifically designed to appeal to vloggers and first-time mirrorless camera buyers due to its compact form factor and advanced video capabilities. Despite its lower price point, it still requires V30 cards for stable video recording performance.

devices.notes: Released late 2024 as Fujifilm's entry-level vlogging and creator-focused camera. High search volume is expected as it gains popularity within the content creation community due to its feature set and affordability.

devices.name: Fujifilm X-T30 II
devices.whySpecs: A mid-range APS-C camera featuring a 26MP sensor and capable of 4K 30fps video recording. V30 cards handle all its recording modes comfortably, making it a reliable choice for both photography and video. It is popular as a more compact and budget-friendly alternative to the larger, flagship X-T5 models.

faq.q: X-T30 II vs X-T5 - do I need faster cards?
faq.a: No, the X-T30 II uses a UHS-I card slot and requires V30 cards, which are sufficient for its capabilities. In contrast, the X-T5 features faster UHS-II slots and can benefit from V60 or even V90 cards due to its higher resolution and more demanding video modes. If you're on a budget, the X-T30 II saves money on both the camera body and compatible SD cards.

devices.notes: A popular mid-range Fujifilm camera known for its compact size and strong image quality. Good availability on the used market makes it a compelling option. Features a single SD UHS-I card slot.

devices.name: Fujifilm X-T50
devices.whySpecs: Fujifilm's latest mid-range APS-C camera, boasting a 40MP sensor and 6.2K video recording capabilities. A V60 speed class card is essential to ensure reliable performance for its high-resolution video and fast burst shooting modes. Its UHS-II slot provides faster data transfers and buffer clearing compared to models with only UHS-I slots.

faq.q: Is the Fujifilm X-T50 the X-T5 in a smaller body?
faq.a: Mostly. It has the same 40MP sensor and processor, but one SD slot instead of two. The same V60 cards work in both.

devices.notes: Released in 2024 as a compact alternative to the X-T5, appealing to enthusiasts seeking top-tier image quality in a more portable form factor. It is gaining popularity and is expected to have high search volume.

devices.name: Sony FX30

sdCard.type: Dual slots: CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II
sdCard.minSpeed: V60 (SD), V90 recommended for high bitrates

devices.whySpecs: A professional cinema camera in Super 35 (APS-C) format, capable of 6K oversampled 4K recording. Both card slots accept either CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II cards. For the highest bitrate ALL-I codec and extended takes, V90 SD cards or CFexpress Type A cards are recommended to ensure stable recording and optimal performance.

faq.q: Should I use CFexpress Type A or SD cards in the FX30?
faq.a: For most common shooting scenarios and high-quality recording, V90 SD cards are perfectly sufficient and significantly more affordable. CFexpress Type A is primarily necessary for the absolute highest bitrate ALL-I recording codecs, or when you require the fastest possible offload speeds to your computer. You can start with V90 SD and only upgrade to CFexpress if you encounter specific performance limitations.

faq.q: Can I mix CFexpress Type A and SD cards in the FX30?
faq.a: Yes, you can use one CFexpress Type A card and one SD UHS-II card simultaneously. This offers a flexible and cost-effective approach: you can record your primary footage to the faster CFexpress card and use the SD card for overflow or backup. Both slots are identical in their physical interface and interchangeable for either card type.

devices.notes: A highly popular professional cinema camera among indie filmmakers and YouTube creators. Its dual CFexpress Type A / SD UHS-II slots offer versatile media options. Shares similar media requirements with its full-frame counterpart, the FX3.

devices.name: Sony FX3

sdCard.type: Dual slots: CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II

devices.whySpecs: Sony's full-frame cinema camera, known for its outstanding 4K 120fps capability. V90 SD cards are essential for reliably recording high frame rate footage and using ALL-I codecs. While CFexpress Type A cards provide the absolute maximum performance, they come at a premium cost.

faq.q: Do the Sony FX3 and FX30 use the same cards?
faq.a: Yes. Both have two slots that take CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II, with V90 needed for All-Intra.

faq.q: Do I need a V90 SD card for the FX3, or is V60 enough?
faq.a: V60 covers standard 4K. 4K/120 and XAVC S-I All-Intra need V90 or CFexpress Type A.

devices.notes: A professional full-frame cinema camera, often considered the video-centric version of the A7S III. It features dual CFexpress Type A / SD UHS-II slots, making it very popular with serious videographers and filmmakers for its robust video features.

devices.name: Fujifilm X-E5
devices.whySpecs: A compact, rangefinder-style camera featuring a 40.2MP X-Trans CMOS 5 HR sensor and capable of 6.2K video recording. V30 cards handle both 4K and 6.2K recording reliably. Its UHS-II slot supports faster sustained write speeds for higher bitrate footage and quicker buffer clearing during burst shooting.

faq.q: What is the key difference between the X-E5 and the X-M5?
faq.a: The X-E5 is designed with a traditional rangefinder-style body, featuring a centered electronic viewfinder. In contrast, the X-M5 is more vlog-focused and typically features a vari-angle or flip screen. Both cameras share identical SD card requirements, needing a V30 minimum. Your choice between them should be based on your preferred shooting style and ergonomic preferences, rather than card specifications.

faq.q: Do I need a UHS-II card, or will UHS-I work?
faq.a: UHS-I V30 cards meet the camera's minimum requirement and work for 4K/6.2K recording. The X-E5's slot is UHS-II compliant, so upgrading to a UHS-II card gives faster buffer clearing after bursts and quicker file transfers, but it is not required for in-camera recording.

devices.notes: Released in 2025 as a compact, rangefinder-style option within the Fujifilm X-series lineup. It targets street photographers and enthusiasts who prefer a lightweight camera with classic aesthetics.
devices.metaDescription: The Fujifilm X-E5 shoots up to 6.2K video from a 40.2MP sensor. Its UHS-II slot and V30 card handle both high-res stills and 6.2K reliably.

devices.name: Fujifilm X100V
devices.whySpecs: The previous-generation premium compact camera with a fixed 23mm f/2 lens and a 26MP sensor. A V30 speed class card handles 4K 30fps video recording comfortably. Despite being superseded by the X100VI, it remains extremely popular on the used market due to its iconic design and image quality.

faq.q: Are the SD card requirements the same for the X100V and the X100VI?
faq.a: No, the X100VI requires V60 UHS-II cards for its higher-resolution 6.2K video recording capabilities. The X100V, in contrast, maxes out at 4K 30fps and only requires V30 UHS-I cards. This difference in card speed requirements means the older X100V can be a more budget-friendly option for both the camera and its accessories.

faq.q: Why is the Fujifilm X100V still so expensive on the used market?
faq.a: The X100 series experienced a viral surge in popularity on social media platforms, creating immense demand for these cameras. Coupled with the X100VI being perennially sold out, used X100V prices have remained remarkably high. It's still an excellent camera that offers a premium experience with more modest card requirements than its successor.

devices.notes: Previous-generation X100 model. Despite its age, it is still massively popular and often sells at a high price on the used market. High ongoing search volume is driven by the scarcity of the X100VI, pushing buyers towards its still-capable predecessor.

faq.q: Is the Fujifilm X-T3 still worth buying used?
faq.a: Yes, on a budget. It records 4K/60 10-bit internally and has two SD UHS-II slots.

faq.q: Do I need V90 cards for the X-T3?
faq.a: Only for 400 Mbps All-Intra. V60 covers every other mode.

devices.notes: A very popular used camera from its release in 2018. It still boasts an active user community and offers high search volume from buyers looking for a powerful camera at a budget-friendly price. Features dual SD UHS-II slots.

devices.name: Leica Q3

faq.q: Does the Leica Q3 shoot 8K video?
faq.a: Yes, 8K/30. It also records 4K/60 and ProRes 422 HQ. Use a V90 UHS-II card for ProRes.

faq.q: Is the Leica Q3 worth its price?
faq.a: For street and travel photographers who want a fixed 28mm f/1.7, many think so. For cards, budget for a fast UHS-II card, since there's only one slot.

devices.notes: Leica's flagship compact camera. Extremely expensive but highly sought-after for its unique blend of traditional aesthetics and modern performance. Single SD UHS-II card slot; no 8K video mode.
devices.metaDescription: The Leica Q3 records 8K/30 and ProRes to one SD UHS-II slot. V60 covers stills and most video; buy V90 for ProRes. Best cards for the Q3.

faq.q: Do the Leica Q3 43 and Q3 use the same SD card?
faq.a: Yes. Same sensor, same processor, same single SD UHS-II slot.

devices.notes: Released in 2024 as a 43mm variant of the Q3, offering a different perspective for photographers. Same single SD UHS-II slot and 4K/30p video ceiling as the standard Q3.

devices.name: Leica M11

faq.q: Does the Leica M11 record video?
faq.a: No. The M11 is a stills-only rangefinder.

faq.q: Does the Leica M11 have internal storage?
faq.a: Yes, 64GB. You can save to the card, to internal memory, or to both as a backup.

devices.notes: Leica's flagship digital M-series rangefinder camera. It combines classic design with modern digital capabilities. Features a single SD UHS-II slot and is renowned for its high-resolution sensor.

devices.name: Leica Q2

faq.q: Should I buy a Leica Q2 or the newer Q3?
faq.a: The Q3 adds a 60MP sensor, 8K video and a tilting screen. The Q2 costs less used. Both have one SD UHS-II slot.

devices.notes: The previous-generation Q-series model from Leica. It is still highly sought-after on the used market for its exceptional image quality and user experience. Features a single SD UHS-II slot, unlike the Q3 which has dual slots.

faq.q: Is the Leica D-Lux 8 a rebadged Panasonic?
faq.a: It shares its platform with the Panasonic Lumix LX100 II, with Leica's own design and menus. Card needs are the same: V30 UHS-I.

devices.notes: Released in 2024, the Leica D-Lux 8 is a new compact camera that continues Leica's partnership with Panasonic. It's often considered a premium point-and-shoot option. Features a single SD UHS-I slot.

devices.name: Leica M10
devices.whySpecs: A previous-generation digital rangefinder camera from Leica, featuring a 24MP sensor. A V30 speed class card is sufficient for all its shooting modes, including high-resolution stills. It embodies the classic Leica M experience in a digital body, making it a desirable option on the used market.

faq.q: Is the Leica M10 still worth buying used in 2024?
faq.a: For photographers seeking the classic Leica rangefinder experience at a more accessible price point than the newer M11, the M10 is an excellent used purchase. It continues to deliver outstanding image quality and the unique M-series handling. With V30 UHS-I cards being perfectly adequate, it also represents a more cost-effective media solution.

devices.notes: A previous-generation M-series digital rangefinder camera. Still highly regarded and popular among enthusiasts and collectors. Features a single SD UHS-I slot.

devices.name: Panasonic Lumix S9
devices.whySpecs: Panasonic's new compact full-frame camera, specifically aimed at content creators, featuring 6K video recording and advanced stabilization. A V60 speed class card handles standard video recording reliably, but a V90 card is recommended for the highest quality recording modes and high frame rates. Its single SD UHS-II slot contributes to its compact body design.

faq.q: Is the Lumix S9 good for vlogging?
faq.a: Yes. It is Panasonic's smallest full-frame body, with in-body stabilization and LUT support. It has one SD slot, so carry a spare card.

devices.notes: Released in 2024, the Lumix S9 is a significant new entry in the full-frame mirrorless market, targeting content creators and vloggers. Its compact form factor and advanced video features are key selling points. Features a single SD UHS-II slot.

devices.name: Panasonic Lumix S5 IIX
searchTerms: panasonic lumix s5 iix sd card
devices.whySpecs: The S5 IIX records 6K and 4K in All-Intra and ProRes, and outputs RAW over HDMI to an external recorder. The high-bitrate internal modes need V90 cards. It can also record to a USB-C SSD.

faq.q: What is the difference in SD card requirements between the S5 IIX and the regular S5 II?
faq.a: The Lumix S5 IIX specifically requires V90 cards for its advanced internal ProRes and external RAW video recording capabilities, which the standard S5 II does not offer. While the standard S5 II works perfectly with V60 cards for its maximum video quality, if you're purchasing the 'X' model specifically for its professional video codecs, it is critical to use V90 cards to ensure stable recording and avoid dropped frames.

devices.notes: The video-centric variant of the Lumix S5 II. Its internal ProRes and RAW recording capabilities make it a formidable tool for professional videographers and filmmakers. Its demanding video codecs necessitate the use of V90 cards. Features dual SD UHS-II slots.

devices.name: Panasonic Lumix S5 II
searchTerms: panasonic lumix s5 ii sd card
devices.whySpecs: The S5 II records 6K and 4K/60 with phase-detect autofocus. A V60 card handles standard 4K and 6K modes. For All-Intra, use V90.

faq.q: Is the Lumix S5 II good for both photography and video?
faq.a: Yes, the Lumix S5 II is widely considered one of the best hybrid cameras available, offering a strong balance of features for both stills and video. Its advanced autofocus system and comprehensive video codecs make it a highly capable tool for diverse creative tasks. V60 cards provide all the necessary speed and reliability for demanding photo burst sequences and high-resolution video recording.

devices.notes: A very popular hybrid full-frame mirrorless camera. It is highly regarded for its performance, features, and competitive pricing. Features dual SD UHS-II slots, offering reliability and flexibility for professional use.

devices.name: Nikon D7500
devices.whySpecs: The D7500 is a 20MP APS-C DSLR with 4K/30 video and 8 fps bursts. It has one SD UHS-I slot, unlike the dual-slot D7200 and D500. A U3/V30 card covers video and bursts.

faq.q: Is the Nikon D7500 still a good camera?
faq.a: Yes, for DSLR shooters on a budget. Its autofocus and battery life hold up well.

faq.q: Does the Nikon D7500 have two SD card slots?
faq.a: No, it has one. The D7200 before it had two. Back up after each shoot.

devices.notes: A popular APS-C DSLR from its release in 2017. It is still widely used by enthusiasts and semi-professionals for its strong performance. It has a strong presence on the used market. Features dual SD UHS-I slots.

devices.name: Nikon Zf
devices.whySpecs: The Zf records 4K/30 oversampled from 6K, or 4K/60 in DX crop, and 1080p/120. Slot 1 takes SD UHS-II and slot 2 takes microSD UHS-I. A V30 card covers video; a fast UHS-II card in slot 1 clears the buffer quickest. When you record to both slots, the slower microSD card sets the pace.

faq.q: What card slots does the Nikon Zf have?
faq.a: One SD UHS-II slot and one microSD UHS-I slot. Use the SD slot for primary recording and the microSD for backup.

faq.q: Do I need V90 cards for the Nikon Zf?
faq.a: No. The Zf tops out at 4K/60 in DX crop and doesn't record RAW video internally. V30 covers it; V60 adds headroom.

devices.notes: Released in late 2023, the Nikon Zf has become a highly popular retro-styled full-frame mirrorless camera. It shares core technology with the Z6 III, offering strong performance in a distinct aesthetic package. Features dual SD UHS-II slots.
devices.metaDescription: The Nikon Zf has an SD UHS-II slot and a microSD UHS-I slot. A V30 card covers its 4K video; the microSD slot is slower. Best cards for both.

devices.name: Nikon Z50 II
devices.whySpecs: Nikon's APS-C mirrorless camera has a 20.9MP sensor and a single SD UHS-I slot. U3/V30 cards cover 4K video. For bursts at 11 fps, the card's write speed decides how fast the buffer clears, so a faster UHS-I card helps photographers more than videographers.

faq.q: Do the Nikon Z50 II and the original Z50 use the same SD card?
faq.a: Yes, both take SD UHS-I cards, and V30 covers both. The Z50 II adds 4K/60 and 10-bit N-Log, which a V30 card still handles.

devices.notes: Released in late 2024 as an updated version of the popular Z50. It targets beginners, vloggers, and photographers seeking a compact and capable mirrorless camera. Features a single SD UHS-I slot.
devices.metaDescription: The Nikon Z50 II takes SD UHS-I cards. A U3/V30 card covers 4K/60 video; a faster UHS-I card clears the buffer quicker after bursts. Best cards.

devices.name: Nikon Z6 III

sdCard.minSpeed: V60 (SD), V90 for high frame rate video

devices.whySpecs: Nikon's latest full-frame hybrid camera, featuring a partially stacked sensor and advanced video capabilities, including 6K RAW. V90 SD cards or CFexpress Type B cards are recommended for demanding tasks like 4K 120fps and N-RAW recording. Its dual slot design provides both redundancy and versatility for professional workflows.

faq.q: Should I use CFexpress Type B or SD cards in the Nikon Z6 III?
faq.a: For most users, high-quality V90 SD cards in both slots are often sufficient for excellent performance. However, CFexpress Type B cards are necessary for the absolute highest bitrate N-RAW recording and for maximizing burst depth during intense sports photography. You can start with V90 SD cards and only consider upgrading to CFexpress if your specific professional workflow demands it.

faq.q: Can I mix CFexpress Type B and SD cards in the Z6 III?
faq.a: Yes, the Nikon Z6 III is designed with a hybrid dual slot: Slot 1 accepts CFexpress Type B, and Slot 2 accepts SD UHS-II. This configuration is highly flexible and cost-effective. You can use a faster CFexpress card in Slot 1 for primary recording (e.g., RAW video) and an SD card in Slot 2 for backup or less demanding tasks (e.g., JPEG photos or 4K video).

devices.notes: Released mid-2024 as the flagship hybrid successor to the Z6 II. It is very popular with photo/video hybrid shooters due to its advanced sensor and robust video features. Features a CFexpress Type B slot and an SD UHS-II slot.

faq.q: Is the Nikon Z6 II still a good buy compared to the Z6 III?
faq.a: Yes, on a budget. The Z6 III adds 6K N-RAW and a faster sensor; the Z6 II has the same slot layout: CFexpress Type B plus SD UHS-II.

devices.notes: A popular hybrid full-frame mirrorless camera from its release in 2020. It's highly regarded for its balance of image quality, video features, and ergonomics. Features dual SD UHS-II slots for reliable data management.
devices.metaDescription: The Nikon Z6 II has a CFexpress Type B/XQD slot and an SD UHS-II slot. A V60 SD card covers 4K/60; CFexpress clears bursts fastest. Best cards.

faq.q: Is the Nikon D850 still worth using?

faq.q: Do I need XQD cards, or are SD cards enough for the D850?
faq.a: SD works; XQD or CFexpress clears the buffer faster. For long 7 to 9 fps RAW bursts, use slot 1.

faq.q: Can I use CFexpress cards in the D850's XQD slot?

devices.name: Nikon D750
devices.whySpecs: A popular full-frame DSLR from 2014, featuring a 24MP sensor and 1080p video recording. Class 10 (U1) cards are sufficient for photography, while U3 (V30) is recommended for 1080p 60fps video to ensure stability. Its dual SD slots enable convenient backup recording or overflow for extended shooting sessions.

faq.q: Is the Nikon D750 still worth buying used in 2024?
faq.a: Yes, for budget-conscious photographers seeking an excellent full-frame DSLR, the D750 remains a fantastic value. It delivers superb image quality, comfortable ergonomics, and the legendary battery life characteristic of Nikon DSLRs. Used prices are very affordable, and basic Class 10 or U3 SD cards work perfectly, keeping the total cost of ownership low.

faq.q: Do I need fast SD cards for the Nikon D750?
faq.a: No, the D750's specifications do not demand high-speed cards like V60 or V90. A Class 10 (U1) card is perfectly adequate for photos and casual 1080p video. A U3 (V30) card offers improved reliability for 1080p 60fps video recording but isn't strictly necessary. You can effectively focus your budget on quality lenses rather than expensive, ultra-fast cards.

devices.notes: An extremely popular full-frame DSLR that continues to see significant activity on the used market. It is highly regarded for its excellent value proposition and performance. Features dual SD UHS-I slots.

devices.name: Nikon Z5
devices.whySpecs: The Z5 shoots 4K video and features dual UHS-II slots. While V30 cards can work for some video modes, V60 is recommended for maximum reliability across all recording formats and for clearing the buffer faster during burst shooting.

faq.q: Do I need two cards for the Nikon Z5?
faq.a: Not required. Two cards let you record a backup, overflow when one fills, or split RAW and JPEG.

devices.notes: Nikon's popular entry-level full-frame camera. Its dual UHS-II slots are a major selling point in its class.

devices.name: Canon EOS R100
devices.whySpecs: The R100 is Canon's most budget-friendly RF camera and shoots 4K video (with a crop). A V30 card is required to ensure stable 4K video recording without errors.

faq.q: Is the Canon R100 a good first camera?
faq.a: Yes, it is designed specifically for beginners. It's very affordable and provides a simple entry into Canon's modern mirrorless system. For its 4K video mode, be sure to get a V30-rated SD card.

devices.notes: Canon's cheapest RF mount camera, targeting first-time buyers.

faq.q: Do I need a CFexpress Type A card for the A7R V?
faq.a: For 8K video and maximum burst shooting performance, yes. For general photography and 4K video, a fast V90 SD card will work well and is more cost-effective. The dual combo slots give you the flexibility to choose.

faq.q: Can I mix a slow SD card with a fast XQD or CFexpress card?
faq.a: You can, but it may create a bottleneck in certain recording modes. When you configure the camera to write the same data to both slots for backup, the overall speed is limited by the slower card. For maximum performance, pair your D500 with a fast card in each slot or use the second slot for JPEGs and the primary slot for RAW.

devices.notes: Flagship APS-C DSLR with one XQD/CFexpress Type B slot and one SD UHS-II slot. Later firmware added CFexpress Type B support alongside XQD.

devices.name: Raspberry Pi 5
devices.whySpecs: The Raspberry Pi 5 boots its operating system from the microSD card, and it's the first Pi that can read one quickly: the Pi 5's SD interface supports SDR104, roughly doubling the bus speed to about 100 MB/s versus the ~50 MB/s ceiling on the Pi 4. To see that, you need a UHS-I card that's rated for it. A slow card is the single most common cause of a Pi 5 that feels sluggish. Beyond raw throughput, look for an A2 rating: the 'A' (Application Performance Class) ratings describe random read/write speed, which is what an operating system does all day, and unlike the Pi 4 the Pi 5 supports the command queuing that lets A2 cards deliver on it. If you need more speed than any microSD can give, the Pi 5's PCIe connector accepts an M.2 HAT and NVMe SSD.

faq.q: What's more important for the Raspberry Pi 5, V30 or A2?
faq.a: The A2 rating is more important. The 'V' rating (e.g., V30) is for sustained video recording speed, while the 'A' rating (Application Performance Class) is for random read/write operations, which is what an operating system does. An A2 card will feel much faster in daily use.

faq.q: Is an A2 card worth it on the Pi 5, or is A1 fine?
faq.a: On the Pi 5, A2 is worth paying for, which was not true on the Pi 4. A2 cards get their speed advantage from command queuing, and the Pi 4's SD host support never took advantage of it, so A2 cards there performed much like A1. The Pi 5 changed that, and it also raised the bus speed to SDR104 (~100 MB/s vs ~50 MB/s). If you're reusing a card from an older Pi, that's the upgrade you'd feel.

faq.q: Should I use an NVMe SSD instead of a microSD card on the Pi 5?
faq.a: If your project is disk-heavy, yes. The Pi 5 added a PCIe connector, so with an M.2 HAT you can boot from an NVMe SSD several times faster than any microSD card, with far better write endurance. A good microSD card is still the simpler and cheaper choice for general desktop use, learning projects, and anything you'll reimage often.

devices.notes: Targets a huge DIY and technical audience. The card is a mandatory component.

sdCard.type: microSDXC (on carrier board, when not using onboard eMMC)

devices.whySpecs: The CM5 is a System-on-Module sold with 0GB (Lite), 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of onboard eMMC for builders who order it that way. If you're using the Lite SKU with a carrier board's microSD slot instead, this is not a desktop Pi 5 install card. CM5 boards are overwhelmingly deployed as embedded/server hardware running persistent logging, local databases, or always-on services. That workload is continuous overwrite, not occasional boot reads. Ignore A1/A2 speed-class shopping advice here and pick a card rated for sustained write endurance (TBW), the same logic used for dash cams and surveillance recorders, or budget for the onboard eMMC SKU if your carrier board supports it.

faq.q: Should I buy the CM5 with onboard eMMC or use a microSD card?
faq.a: Onboard eMMC is more durable and faster for continuous server workloads if your carrier board and budget support it. If you go with the Lite (0GB) SKU and a microSD card instead, treat the card like dash-cam storage: prioritize write endurance (TBW) over speed class.

faq.q: Do I need a V30 or A2 card for the Compute Module 5?
faq.a: No. Those speed classes target desktop responsiveness and video bitrate, not this device's actual use case. CM5 boards are typically embedded/server builds running logging or databases 24/7. A High Endurance card (SanDisk MAX ENDURANCE, Samsung PRO Endurance) will outlast a standard A2 card by years under that write pattern.

devices.name: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
devices.whySpecs: Like all Raspberry Pis, the Pi 4 runs its OS from the microSD card, so random access speed, not video throughput, is what makes it feel fast. That's the A (Application Performance Class) rating, and an A1 card is the spec that matters here. Paying extra for A2 on a Pi 4 is usually wasted money: A2's advantage comes from command queuing, which the Pi 4's SD host support doesn't take advantage of, so A2 cards generally perform about the same as A1 on this board. The Pi 4's card interface also tops out around 50 MB/s regardless of how fast the card is rated, so a premium high-speed card won't stretch its legs. Save the A2 and SDR104 spending for a Pi 5.

faq.q: Is a V30 card good for a Raspberry Pi 4?
faq.a: A V30 rating is not the most important spec. Look for an A1 or A2 rating instead. The V30 rating is for video and doesn't affect OS performance. The Application Performance Class (A1/A2) is what makes the Pi 4 feel fast and responsive.

faq.q: What is the minimum recommended capacity for Raspberry Pi 4?
faq.a: A 32GB card is a good minimum for Raspberry Pi OS with a desktop environment. This leaves enough space for installing several applications and for project files. For more complex projects or storing media, 64GB or larger is recommended.

faq.q: Will a faster card make my Raspberry Pi 4 faster?
faq.a: Only up to a point. The Pi 4's SD card interface runs at roughly 50 MB/s, so once your card comfortably clears that, a faster rating on the label buys you nothing on this board. Moving from a cheap no-name card to a decent A1 card is a real, noticeable upgrade; moving from a good A1 card to a premium A2 one generally isn't. The Pi 5 raised that ceiling to about 100 MB/s and added the A2 support the Pi 4 lacks.

devices.notes: Still one of the most popular SBCs in the world. The distinction between video speed (V) and application speed (A) is a key point for users.

Official documentation for related Orange Pi 5 boards lists 128GB as the supported microSD size, but many users successfully run 256GB and even 512GB cards, making 32–128GB a safe, mainstream choice and larger cards a practical but unofficial option.

faq.q: Do I need a V30 video card for Orange Pi 5?
faq.a: No, a V30 card is not required for most Orange Pi 5 use cases. The board cares far more about random I/O for the operating system than about sustained video write speed. A Class 10 / U1 card with an A1 or A2 rating is usually the best balance of price and performance.

faq.q: What capacity microSD card should I choose for Orange Pi 5?
faq.a: For a typical Linux desktop or server image, 32GB or 64GB is plenty. If you plan to store many Docker images, databases, or media files directly on the card, 128GB gives more breathing room. Larger cards (256GB or 512GB) often work, but they go beyond the capacities mentioned in many Orange Pi hardware parameter sheets.

faq.q: Is microSD slower than NVMe or eMMC on Orange Pi 5?
faq.a: Yes, microSD is the slowest storage option on the board. It is perfectly fine for experimenting, lightweight servers, and small desktops, but for heavy I/O workloads or large databases it is worth migrating the root filesystem to an NVMe SSD or eMMC module and keeping the microSD only as a boot or recovery medium.

devices.whySpecs: 4K dash cams write about 50 to 100 Mbps depending on the model and codec. V30 guarantees 30 MB/s sustained, above that rate. Loop recording rewrites the whole card over and over, so high-endurance cards, which manufacturers rate in recording hours, outlast standard cards.

faq.q: What's the difference between dash cam and regular microSD cards?
faq.a: Endurance. High-endurance cards are rated for tens of thousands of hours of continuous recording; SanDisk rates its MAX Endurance line at up to 120,000 hours. Standard cards carry no such rating.

faq.q: Can I use a regular fast microSD card in a dash cam?
faq.a: It works, but wears out sooner. Speed doesn't help with constant rewrites. A high-endurance card is the better buy.

faq.q: Is 64GB or 128GB better for a dash cam?
faq.a: 128GB for most drivers. At 4K, 64GB holds roughly 1.5 to 3 hours and 128GB about double. For parking mode, buy 256GB.

devices.notes: Universal dash cam recommendation. Works with Rexing, Viofo, Garmin, VANTRUE, and most aftermarket 4K cameras.

faq.q: Can I use V20 cards with DJI Mini 4 Pro?

faq.q: Do I need a faster card for 4K/100 slow motion or D-Log M?
faq.a: No, a V30 card covers both. The top bitrate is 150 Mbps, about 19 MB/s. Sustained speed matters more than the label: counterfeit cards often pass a quick benchmark and then slow down during a long clip. Buy from a reputable seller and format the card in the drone.

faq.q: Which microSD brands are safest for a drone?
faq.a: SanDisk, Lexar, Samsung and Kingston all appear on DJI's recommended card lists. A card failure mid-flight loses footage you cannot reshoot.

faq.q: Can I reuse an old microSD card in my drone?
faq.a: Only if it is V30 and has never thrown an error. Worn cards fail without warning, and a failure mid-flight means lost footage.

devices.notes: DJI officially recommends V30 cards for safe recording. Test new cards before flights.

faq.q: Does the DJI Avata 2 need an SD card?

devices.name: Nintendo Switch
devices.whySpecs: The original Nintendo Switch is limited to the UHS-I interface with a maximum speed of 104MB/s. UHS-II and SD Express cards are backward compatible and will work, but they downclock to the console's UHS-I speed, so their extra performance is wasted money. The console uses standard microSD/microSDHC/microSDXC cards. V30 rated cards from trusted brands provide the best reliability for downloading large digital libraries. All Nintendo-branded SanDisk microSD cards (Zelda, Pokémon, Mario, etc.) are standard UHS-I format and work perfectly on the original Switch. 2TB microSDXC cards from brands like SanDisk and Silicon Power are commercially available and have been verified to work.

faq.q: Does the Switch support cards larger than 1TB?
faq.a: Yes. 2TB microSDXC cards from SanDisk and other brands work after a Switch system update.

faq.q: Can I use my phone's microSD card in the Switch?
faq.a: Yes. Back up the phone data first: the Switch formats the card and erases it.

faq.q: Do I need a V30 card for the Switch?
faq.a: No. V30 is a video rating. Any U1 or U3 card from a known brand loads games at the console's full speed.

devices.notes: Limited to UHS-I speeds (~104MB/s maximum). V30 is recommended for reliability. Compatible with all officially licensed Nintendo-branded SanDisk microSD cards (Zelda, Pokémon, Mario, Yoshi, Animal Crossing, Fortnite).
devices.metaDescription: The Nintendo Switch tops out at UHS-I speed (104MB/s). UHS-II and SD Express cards work but downclock to UHS-I, so their extra speed is wasted money.

devices.name: Nintendo Switch OLED
devices.whySpecs: The Switch OLED has 64GB of internal storage, double the original model. Like every original Switch, its slot is UHS-I (about 100 MB/s). UHS-II and SD Express cards fit but run at UHS-I speed, so they cost more for nothing.

faq.q: Should I buy a UHS-II card for the Switch OLED?
faq.a: No. The slot is UHS-I, so a UHS-II card loads games no faster.

faq.q: Can I use my original Switch's card in the OLED?

faq.q: What size microSD card should I get for the Switch OLED?

devices.notes: OLED users typically purchase larger cards due to increased digital game library usage. UHS-I only (~104MB/s), despite higher internal storage.
devices.metaDescription: The Switch OLED has a UHS-I microSD slot, like every original Switch. UHS-II and Express cards fit but load no faster. Buy 512GB or 1TB for digital games.

devices.whySpecs: The Steam Deck's microSD slot is UHS-I, so cards top out around 100 MB/s no matter what the label says. Games load from the card in small random reads, which is what the A1 and A2 app ratings measure. 2TB cards such as the SanDisk Extreme and Lexar Play work. microSD prices rose across all capacities in 2026 because of a NAND flash shortage.

faq.q: Can I use fast V60 cards?
faq.a: Yes, but they won't load games any faster. The Steam Deck's UHS-I slot caps reads near 100 MB/s, so a V60 or UHS-II card performs like a good A2 UHS-I card.

faq.q: What is the max SD card size for Steam Deck?
faq.a: 2TB, the microSDXC limit. 2TB cards from SanDisk and Lexar work in both the LCD and OLED models.

faq.q: Does the Steam Deck OLED use a different microSD card?
faq.a: No. The OLED model has the same UHS-I microSD slot as the LCD model, so the same cards work in both.

devices.notes: Steam Deck uses UHS-I only. Any A1 or A2 card is enough, because game loads depend on random reads, not the video speed class. Recommend 256GB+ for game library.
devices.metaDescription: Steam Deck takes UHS-I microSD cards up to 2TB. Buy an A2 card in 512GB or 1TB for your game library; V60 and UHS-II cards load no faster.

faq.q: Should I use a UHS-II card in the ROG Ally?
faq.a: Yes, if load times matter to you. The reader supports UHS-II, so a UHS-II card loads games faster. UHS-I cards work at UHS-I speed.

faq.q: What is the best capacity for the ROG Ally?
faq.a: 512GB or 1TB. Many AAA games take over 100GB.

devices.notes: Heat from the device's exhaust can affect the SD card reader in some units. Using a high-quality, reputable UHS-II card is crucial for both reliability and optimal performance.

faq.q: Will a microSD Express card work in my original Switch or Switch OLED?

faq.q: What microSD card should I buy for Switch 2?

devices.notes: Switch 2 is backward compatible with all standard UHS-I microSD cards from the original Switch.
